title: Build a Platform and Watch It Burn — Michael Forrester, Accenture & Whitney Lee, Datadog
talk_summary: A live workshop where the presenters deliberately attack an agent running in Kubernetes and then layer on infrastructure and AI guardrails to block each attack. The transferable core is defense-in-depth for agents: input filtering before the LLM call, output scrubbing after, MCP/tool authorization via a gateway, and standard K8s admission/runtime controls.

takeaways.technique: Input guardrails before the model call
takeaways.what_they_do: Run a small classifier (LLM Guard/Nemo Guardrails, ~8B params) plus regex on the prompt before it reaches the large model, so blocked requests cost zero tokens.
takeaways.evidence_quote: at this level, it didn't process an 800 billion parameter model. Didn't take any tokens. It got blocked.

takeaways.technique: Output scrubbing as a proxy layer
takeaways.what_they_do: A proxy in front of the model runs LLM Guard to redact sensitive strings from responses before they reach the agent, with a toggle to enable mid-stream.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's a proxy here ... running things through LLM Guard to basically scrub it

takeaways.technique: MCP gateway/registry instead of direct public MCP servers
takeaways.what_they_do: Route tool access through an MCP gateway/registry that whitelists tools per agent, rather than wiring public MCP servers directly; they show an 'evil MCP' tool description that smuggles a second instruction to exfiltrate config.
takeaways.evidence_quote: please don't start with public MCP servers ... get an MCP registry or a gateway
takeaways.numbers: claims 33-40% of public MCP servers have serious vulnerabilities (speaker unsure of exact figure)

takeaways.technique: Admission control + runtime policy for agent-spawned workloads
takeaways.evidence_quote: you don't even want like an ls command to run. So so you want that to be stopped

takeaways.technique: Don't rely on the model to refuse; enforce at infra layer
takeaways.what_they_do: They repeatedly got models to comply with disallowed actions within 20-30 prompts, so they argue guardrails must be deterministic infrastructure, not prompt instructions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you don't want to rely on the model to not do the thing that you don't want it to do

takeaways.technique: Rubric for when to use an agent
takeaways.what_they_do: Three questions before automating: is it a bounded system with known interfaces, is it worth it vs. a human, and does it have a verifiable output.
takeaways.numbers: cites Nvidia CFO: ~70% of AI-done jobs could be done cheaper/more reliably by humans
